summary: Sodium cromoglycate (cromolyn sodium) is a mast cell stabilizer used prophylactically across several formulations: inhaled for asthma prophylaxis, intranasal for allergic rhinitis, ophthalmic for allergic conjunctivitis, and an oral solution for systemic mastocytosis. It prevents the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators from mast cells but has no bronchodilator, antihistamine, or anti-inflammatory steroid activity and does not relieve an established attack. The oral solution (for mastocytosis) is approved in some markets but the oral form is not currently a standard FDA-approved systemic product; this record draws on SmPC/BNF and cromolyn class references.

moa: Sodium cromoglycate stabilizes the membrane of sensitized mast cells, inhibiting the calcium-dependent degranulation that follows antigen-IgE binding. This prevents release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators of the immediate and late allergic response. It has no intrinsic bronchodilator, antihistamine, anticholinergic, vasoconstrictor, or glucocorticoid activity, and therefore works only as a prophylactic agent.

preg: Sodium cromoglycate is poorly absorbed and has a long record of use; it is generally considered low risk in pregnancy and may be used when clearly needed, preferring topical/inhaled routes.
lact: Systemic absorption is minimal and little is expected to reach breast milk; it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Systemic absorption is very low across all routes; no specific renal dose adjustment is required.
hepatic: Systemic absorption is very low; no specific hepatic dose adjustment is required.

missed: Use the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up. Consistent regular use is important for benefit.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely to cause serious harm given the very low systemic absorption; manage symptomatically and supportively. No specific antidote is required.
